text:
iris: Uploaded an nsys profile from prod-serving-1 where we see repeated p99 spikes. Link to trace: s3://redwood-traces/1799991234-prod-nsys.qtreport. Looking at timeline I think memcpy vs kernel ordering is the root cause, maybe plus some CPU preemption.

ben: saw the same. Timeline shows long memcpy blocks on a dedicated copy-engine stream while kernels queue up on compute streams.

iris: exact observation: cudaMemcpyAsync (HtoD) events on stream 2 start at the same time kernels are enqueued on streams 0 and 1, but the kernels don't run until the memcpy finishes. That smells like either default-stream blocking or copy-engine saturation. Example snippet from timeline export: 
```
Time(ms)  Thread  Stream  Kind      Name                     Duration(ms)
10234     4321    2       memcpy    cudaMemcpyAsync HtoD       18.4
10234     4321    0       kernel    matmul_kern              2.1
10252     4321    0       kernel    softmax_kern             1.9
```

sam: can you paste the CPU timeline around the same window? Also what were the batch-size distribution and KV cache hit rate during the run?

iris: CPU shows worker-thread id 4321 sleeping ~50ms around these events, likely a GC or Python scheduler gap. Batch sizes skewed a lot: 80% batch=1, 15% batch=2, 5% >=4. KV cache hit rate ~92% but the prefetch path fires on many requests and copies ~45MB chunks synchronously.

kai: with that batch distribution kernel-launch overheads are impactful, but the memcpy ordering is the immediate blocker. If our prefetch uses the default stream or blocking memcpy, compute will wait. Also check if those buffers are pinned — non-pinned host copies are synchronous and slower.

ben: i suspect the kvcache prefetch path uses `cudaMemcpy` fallback or the default stream. On Maxwell/Turing some copy patterns can serialize compute. Fix is to use a dedicated non-blocking stream and `cudaMemcpyAsync` from pinned staging buffers.

iris: this is the exact command I used to capture the trace: `nsys profile --trace=cuda,cudnn,osrt --stats=true --output=/tmp/prod-run` then `nsys export --report=timeline --output=/tmp/timeline.json`. timeline excerpt pasted above.

sam: memcpy 18ms is huge — how many keys or bytes per prefetch?

iris: ~45MB per keyblock, and prefetch is triggered eagerly at first token for many concurrent requests. That causes large host->device transfers on the spot.

kai: two quick mitigations: 1) switch kvcache prefetch to a dedicated non-blocking CUstream and do async memcpy from pinned staging buffers, 2) chunk prefetch into smaller 8MB windows and interleave with compute where possible, 3) tweak batching heuristic to wait ~5-10ms to coalesce batch=1 into larger batches when QPS allows.

ben: also noticed CPU scheduling gaps — check thread affinity and cgroup configs. We had Docker host-level housekeeping that coincided with some spikes in previous runs. Python GC safepoints lined up with those windows in the CPU trace.

iris: i pushed a test branch that switches kvcache memcpy to async on a separate stream and reduces chunk_size to 8MB. Ran a 30-min A/B: p99 dropped ~42% and mean latency dropped ~12% on canary. New trace uploaded: s3://redwood-traces/1799991240-async-prefetch.qtreport.

deploy-bot: canary deploy finished on 3 hosts :rocket: (build 2026-03-18-1799991241)

sam: nice. can we add a perf regression test that runs an nsys trace under synthetic skewed batch=1 workload so we catch regressions early? also add a config toggle to opt into the new prefetch mode for safety.

iris: yep opening PRs for both (PR: github.com/redwood/repo/pull/487). will include the repro nsys command and a small CI job that runs a 30s p99 smoke with simulated prefetch loads. thanks for the quick inputs :thumbsup:
